name: Jelqing

card.summary: A manual penis-enlargement technique with no published clinical evidence of effect and clinician warnings about tissue injury.
card.note: No clinical studies of jelqing were found; clinicians caution against aggressive manipulation.

quick.overview:
Jelqing is a manual technique in which a man strokes or squeezes a semi-erect penis from base toward the head, with the aim of increasing length or girth. It circulates in looksmaxxing forums under labels such as girthmaxxing and lengthmaxxing.

Many people report personal success online, but Wikipedia states that medical evidence is absent. The only peer-reviewed study in this entry's source set concerns men anxious about penis size and notes that they were more likely to attempt methods such as jelqing; it did not test whether jelqing works.
quick.mechanism: Proponents describe the mechanism as repeated stretching that causes microscopic tears in erectile tissue which then heal larger. Some forum members counter that stretching enlarges existing erectile chambers without adding new ones, lowering tissue density. Neither account has been tested in clinical studies.
quick.risks: Clinicians cited by Wikipedia caution against routine or aggressive jelqing because of possible fibrosis and plaque formation, and the technique may raise the risk of hard flaccid syndrome. Penis size anxiety, which often motivates the practice, has been studied separately as a body dysmorphic concern.

lead: Jelqing, also called milking, is a manual technique that people use in the hope of making the penis longer or thicker. It is done on the semi-erect penis, with the hand moving from base toward the head in a repeated stroking and squeezing motion. Wikipedia lists it, alongside vacuum pumps and traction devices, among the physical (non-surgical) methods of penis enlargement. [1][2]

Users pursue it for the same reason as other enlargement methods: a larger-looking or larger-feeling body part can improve how a man feels about his appearance and his body. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it under labels such as girthmaxxing and lengthmaxxing, with threads ranging from routines and progress reports to warnings, and members disagree about whether any gain lasts. [3][4]

Wikipedia states that medical evidence for the technique is absent, that many people nevertheless report success, and that clinicians caution against routine or aggressive manipulation. [1] The word is described as a corrupted form of the Persian phrase jalq zadan, and the practice is attributed to ancient Arab origins. [1][2]

The research literature sits around the technique rather than on it. Reviews of non-surgical enlargement have examined traction devices, vacuum pumps and injectables, and a large body of work has measured typical penis size and the psychology of men concerned about it, but no clinical study has tested jelqing itself. [9][12][13][14]

angle.text: Practitioners use jelqing in the hope of adding length or girth, and with it greater body confidence. Gains reported in forums are personal accounts; no clinical study has measured the outcome.

paras: Jelqing is performed on the semi-erect penis by moving the hand from base to head with a combined squeezing and stroking motion; it is also called milking. [1] Forum discussions describe it as one of several physical enlargement routes alongside stretchers and pumps. [3] Practitioners in these threads talk about it as a routine kept over weeks or months, and some pair it with other devices. [4]

Wikipedia places it among the physical techniques, which also include vacuum pumping and traction. It notes that traction is the only physical method for which limited scientific evidence of some elongation exists, with studies of traction mostly in men with Peyronie's disease, and that reported lengthening from traction in other men is mixed and sometimes negligible. [2] Wikipedia describes supplements, patches and ointments sold for enlargement as generally considered ineffective, and surgical methods as carrying significant risk. [2]

Wikipedia derives the English word from a Latinized, corrupted form of the Persian phrase jalq zadan, in which jalq refers to masturbation and zadan is an auxiliary verb meaning to strike or throb. [1][2] The same article credits the technique to ancient Arab origins and cites a 2023 Urology review by Li and colleagues, titled Penile and Foreskin Stretching Practices Through Time and Culture, that surveys stretching customs across history. [2][16]

The practice reached a wide English-language audience through online men's health and enlargement forums in the early internet era, alongside the spam-email trade in enlargement pills that Wikipedia dates to the late 1990s and early 2000s. [2] In 2003 a leaked order log for one herbal enlargement product showed roughly 6,000 orders in four weeks, and the US Federal Trade Commission said there was no proof such pills worked as advertised. [2] Those products are separate from jelqing, but they formed the commercial and cultural backdrop in which manual methods were discussed.

Proponents describe jelqing as working like other physical enlargement methods: repeated stretching of the erectile tissue is said to cause microscopic tears that heal and increase the organ's volume. A looksmax.org post sets out this account. [3]

The same post argues that the effect is to enlarge the existing erectile chambers of the corpus cavernosum rather than add new ones, which it says would leave a lower density of erectile tissue for the same absolute size, and it applies the same reasoning to the Bathmate pump. [3] These are forum claims; no clinical study has tested either account.

Other forum replies offer a different explanation for any gain, proposing that prolonged filling of the organ with blood during extended sessions produces slow permanent growth, while jelqing itself is only temporary. [4] No published study has examined this.

Accounts from users describe sessions timed for the morning, kept on alternating days, and sometimes combined with a pump or a clamping device after some weeks. [4] Thread titles on looksmax.org include a self-described complete guide, questions from beginners, progress reports after a few weeks, and a meme title about jelqing for eight hours a day for 25 years. [17][18][19][20] The wiki does not reproduce routines or timings.

A 2011 review in BJU International by Oderda and Gontero looked for evidence on non-invasive penile lengthening and found only about ten articles or abstracts on the subject. They concluded that penile extenders (traction devices) were the best-supported conservative option and that approaches such as vacuum devices, penoscrotal rings and exercises lacked solid evidence. [9]

A 2019 systematic review by Marra, Veale, Muir and colleagues, published in Sexual Medicine Reviews, covered 17 studies of 21 interventions in men with normal-sized penises who wanted a larger one. It found study quality poor; extenders increased flaccid length by under 2 cm, vacuum devices did not increase size, injectables increased girth with a high complication rate, and counselling, when offered, often led men to accept that their size was normal. The authors wrote that injectables and surgery should remain a last option, considered unethical outside clinical trials. Manual exercises such as jelqing were not among the interventions reported. [12]

The American Urological Association has stated since January 1994 that fat injection for girth and division of the suspensory ligament for length have not been shown to be safe or efficacious, and the Sexual Medicine Society of North America advised in 2024 against permanent fillers. [2] Writing in European Urology in 2006, Vardi questioned the ethics of enlargement procedures in men with a normal-sized penis. [2][10]

A 2015 systematic review by Veale and colleagues pooled data from up to 15,521 men to build nomograms of penis size; it reported a mean erect length of 13.12 cm and a mean erect circumference of 11.66 cm, and its most consistent correlation was between height and stretched or erect length. [13] Clinicians who counsel men about size frequently use such norms, and Wikipedia notes that some doctors say most men seeking enlargement have normal-sized penises. [2]

Clinicians cited by Wikipedia caution against routine use, particularly excessive or aggressive manipulation, because of possible fibrosis and plaque formation, and say it may increase the risk of hard flaccid syndrome. [1] Hard flaccid syndrome is a condition described in case series, and a 2026 retrospective series of 32 men reported improvements in erection hardness scores after a multimodal rehabilitation programme; the authors called the findings hypothesis-generating. [15] That series does not establish a link between the condition and any particular practice.

Other methods carry their own documented harms: consumer vacuum pumps can reach pressures that damage tissue, constriction worn for more than 30 minutes can cause permanent damage, and injected silicone has caused infection, necrosis and deformity, including a 2013 cluster of hospitalizations in Vietnam reported by Thanh Nien News. [2][11]

Wylie and Eardley described in a 2007 BJU International paper men who worry that their penis is too small and who may feel ashamed of being seen. They noted that such worry is often within the normal range of male experience but can become excessive, presenting as small penis syndrome with rumination, compulsive checking or body dysmorphic disorder, and recommended thorough assessment and normalizing discussion. [14]

Wikipedia reports that some doctors say most men seeking enlargement have normal-sized penises and may underestimate their own size while overestimating the average, a pattern described as penile dysmorphophobia. [2] A 2015 cohort study of 90 men found that men with body dysmorphic disorder about penis size, and men with small penis anxiety, were more likely than controls to have tried methods such as jelqing, vacuum pumps or stretching devices. [8]

Threads on looksmax.org range from routines and progress reports to warnings. One member plans morning sessions and asks how long to continue and whether to add clamping; replies disagree on whether the practice has a permanent effect. [4] Another thread titled as a warning argues jelqing leaves erectile tissue of lower density. [3] A thread titled around a possible small gain after five weeks shows the kind of tentative self-report common in these communities, and another asks outright whether it works. [17][19]
On T Nation, jelqing has long been a running joke in banter threads, and one 2023 poster in a different thread says daily jelqing and a pump helped with sensitivity. [5][6]

Journalists cited by Wikipedia have described the method as biologically implausible. [1] Hacker News carried a 2026 link to an article titled 'Jelqing: The latest in a long history of attempts to enlarge the male member', indicating press interest in the practice's recent online popularity. [7] A 2025 Sexual Medicine study analysed the text quality and readability of AI-transcribed YouTube videos on penile enlargement, reflecting how much of the public information on the topic is video-based. [21]

No studies found testing jelqing. The nearest research concerns related methods and the psychology of men concerned about size. A 2015 cohort study of 90 men compared men with body dysmorphic disorder concerning penis size, men with small penis anxiety, and controls. It found that men with either concern were more likely than controls to have tried to change penis size or shape, for example by jelqing, vacuum pumps or stretching devices, and reported reduced sexual-function scores in the dysmorphic group. It did not test whether jelqing changes size. [8]

Systematic reviews of non-surgical enlargement have evaluated traction devices, vacuum devices and injectables, with limited elongation reported for extenders and poor-quality evidence overall. [9][12]

timeline.event: The American Urological Association first publishes statements that fat injection and suspensory ligament division for enlargement have not been shown safe or efficacious. [2]
A leaked log shows about 6,000 orders for one herbal enlargement product in four weeks; the US FTC says there is no proof such pills work as advertised. [2]
Vardi publishes an ethics critique of enlargement procedures for men with normal-sized penises in European Urology. [2][10]
Wylie and Eardley describe small penis syndrome in BJU International. [14]
Oderda and Gontero review non-invasive penile lengthening, finding about ten relevant articles. [9]
Veale and colleagues publish size nomograms from up to 15,521 men; a cohort study reports men with penis-size body dysmorphic disorder are more likely to have tried methods such as jelqing. [8][13]
Marra and colleagues publish a systematic review of interventions in men with normal penis size; print issue January 2020. [12]
Li and colleagues publish a Urology review of penile and foreskin stretching practices across cultures. [16]
The Sexual Medicine Society of North America publishes a position statement on cosmetic penile enhancement, advising against permanent fillers. [2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, jelqing is discussed both as a size-increase method and as a practice some members warn against, with members disagreeing about whether any gain is permanent. On T Nation it is mostly a recurring joke. [3][4][5]

claims.claim: Jelqing stretches erectile tissue, causing microtears that heal into a larger penis.
claims.believers: Proponents describe repeated stretching of erectile tissue as the route to growth, in the same way as other physical enlargement methods. [3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states medical evidence for jelqing is absent and that journalists have called the method biologically implausible. [1] No clinical studies of jelqing were found.

claims.claim: Jelqing and similar methods enlarge the existing erectile chambers without adding new ones, lowering erectile tissue density.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org post argues that the tissue around the chambers also expands, leaving lower-density erectile tissue, and applies the same reasoning to pumps and stretchers. [3]
claims.experts: No published study has measured erectile tissue density after jelqing; clinicians cited on Wikipedia instead raise fibrosis and plaque formation as possible harms. [1]

claims.claim: Any gain from jelqing is only temporary.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org thread says jelqing is only temporary, while claiming prolonged engorgement leads to slow permanent growth. [4]
claims.experts: No published study has measured durable size change from jelqing. [1]

claims.believers: Some forum members warn that manual stretching can injure the organ. [3]
claims.experts: Clinicians cited by Wikipedia caution against aggressive jelqing because of possible fibrosis and plaque formation and a possible link to hard flaccid syndrome. [1]

claims.claim: Traction devices (stretchers) are the proven version of manual stretching.
claims.believers: Forum members group jelqing with stretchers and pumps as physical methods, and some treat devices as the more serious option. [3]
claims.experts: Oderda and Gontero concluded in 2011 that extenders were the best-supported non-invasive option, while Marra and colleagues in 2019 reported flaccid length gains under 2 cm from extenders in poor-quality studies. [9][12]

claims.believers: A 2023 T Nation poster credits a pump and daily jelqing with improved sensitivity rather than size. [6]
claims.experts: The 2019 systematic review reported that vacuum devices did not increase size, and Wikipedia notes consumer pumps can reach pressures that damage tissue. [2][12]

claims.claim: Men who want enlargement mostly have a normal-sized penis.
claims.believers: Many forum members describe size as a central concern of their appearance and confidence. [4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that some doctors say most men seeking enlargement have normal-sized penises, and a 2015 cohort study found size-anxious men more likely to try methods such as jelqing. [2][8]
